geometric-001.question: Light with a vacuum wavelength of 600 nm enters glass with a refractive index of 1.5. Which correctly describes its wavelength and frequency inside the glass?
choices: The wavelength becomes 900 nm and the frequency is unchanged
The wavelength becomes 400 nm and the frequency is unchanged
The wavelength stays 600 nm and the frequency becomes 1/1.5 of its value
geometric-001.explanation: The speed of light in a medium is v = c/n, so in glass with an index of 1.5 it is 1/1.5 of its vacuum value. Because the number of wave crests is conserved across the boundary, the frequency ν does not change, and the wavelength shrinks to λ = v/ν = λ₀/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. 900 nm comes from multiplying by the index instead of dividing. Thinking that the frequency (and the photon energy hν) changes in a medium is another common misconception: color and photon energy are unchanged when light enters a material. This is why waveguide design uses the “wavelength in the medium”, λ₀/n.

geometric-002.question: Light is incident from air (refractive index 1.0) onto glass with a refractive index of 1.5 at an angle of incidence of 30°. Which value is closest to the angle of refraction?
choices: About 19.5°
About 48.6°
About 30° (the same as the angle of incidence)
geometric-002.explanation: From Snell's law, n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, sinθ₂ = 1.0 × sin30° / 1.5 = 0.5 / 1.5 ≈ 0.333, so θ₂ ≈ 19.5°. Light entering a higher-index medium bends toward the normal. About 48.6° is what you get by multiplying the indices the wrong way round, sinθ₂ = 1.5 × 0.5; it corresponds to bending away from the normal, which happens when light goes from a higher-index to a lower-index medium. The angle is unchanged only when the indices on both sides are equal. Note also that angles are always measured from the normal, not from the surface.

geometric-003.question: When light travels from glass with a refractive index of 1.5 into air (refractive index 1.0), which value is closest to the critical angle (measured from the normal) at which total internal reflection begins?
choices: About 48.2°
About 33.7°
About 41.8°
geometric-003.explanation: The critical angle θc is the angle of incidence at which the refraction angle reaches 90°: sinθc = n₂/n₁ = 1.0/1.5 ≈ 0.667, so θc ≈ 41.8°. At larger angles of incidence there is no transmitted light and all the energy is reflected (an evanescent wave penetrates beyond the boundary but carries no energy away). About 48.2° is the complement, 90° minus the critical angle, and confuses an angle measured from the surface with one measured from the normal. About 33.7° is the angle from tanθ = 1/1.5, which mixes this up with the Brewster-angle calculation (tanθB = n₂/n₁). Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from the higher-index side toward the lower-index side.

geometric-004.question: An object is placed 150 mm in front of a thin convex lens with a focal length of 50 mm. Which correctly gives the image position and lateral magnification? (A real image has a negative magnification.)
choices: 75 mm behind the lens, an inverted real image with magnification −0.5
37.5 mm behind the lens, an inverted real image with magnification −0.25
100 mm behind the lens, an inverted real image with magnification −2
geometric-004.explanation: From the thin-lens equation 1/a + 1/b = 1/f (a is the object distance, b the image distance), 1/b = 1/50 − 1/150 = 2/150, so b = 75 mm. The lateral magnification is m = −b/a = −75/150 = −0.5: an inverted real image half the size of the object. 37.5 mm comes from the sign error 1/b = 1/50 + 1/150. When the object is farther than twice the focal length (100 mm), the image forms between f and 2f and is reduced. A magnification of −2 occurs in the opposite case, when the object is placed between f and 2f (at 75 mm).

geometric-005.question: A lens used in air has an image-side numerical aperture NA of 0.25. Which value is closest to its f-number? Use the relation F ≈ 1/(2NA).
choices: About 4
About 0.5
About 2
geometric-005.explanation: The numerical aperture is NA = n sinθ (θ is the half-angle between the optical axis and the marginal ray), and the f-number is the focal length divided by the entrance-pupil diameter; for a lens that satisfies the sine condition, F ≈ 1/(2NA). With NA = 0.25, F ≈ 1/(2 × 0.25) = 2. About 4 is 1/NA with the factor of 2 dropped, and about 0.5 is 2NA with the reciprocal forgotten. A larger NA (smaller f-number) means a wider cone of light, a brighter image and a smaller diffraction-limited spot, but makes aberration correction harder and the depth of focus shallower.

geometric-006.question: Some oil-immersion microscope objectives have a numerical aperture above 1 (for example 1.4). Why is this possible?
choices: Because the oil amplifies the light from the sample and brightens it, so the sine of the collection angle effectively exceeds 1
Because NA = n sinθ, and the space between the sample and the lens is filled with oil of index about 1.5
Because NA is set by the ratio of focal length to aperture, not by the medium's refractive index, so a larger aperture pushes NA above 1
geometric-006.explanation: The numerical aperture NA = n sinθ includes the refractive index n of the medium on the object side. In air (n = 1), sinθ < 1 keeps NA below 1, but with immersion oil of index about 1.52, θ = 67° gives 1.52 × sin67° ≈ 1.4. sinθ itself never exceeds 1, and oil does not amplify light. Thinking that NA depends only on the ratio of focal length to aperture stretches the approximate relation with the f-number to ignore the medium. Because resolution scales with λ/NA, oil immersion raises resolving power and also prevents light loss from total internal reflection at the cover-glass surface.

geometric-007.question: When white light is focused with a single lens, the focal position shifts with color. What is the main cause of this chromatic aberration?
choices: The lens surfaces are spherical, so rays passing near the edge are bent more strongly
Light is diffracted by the lens aperture
The refractive index of the lens material depends on wavelength (dispersion)
geometric-007.explanation: The refractive index of glass increases at shorter wavelengths (normal dispersion), so blue light is bent more strongly and a convex lens focuses blue in front of red. This is axial (longitudinal) chromatic aberration. Low dispersion is expressed by a high Abbe number, and an achromat — a convex and a concave lens with different Abbe numbers cemented together — brings two wavelengths to the same focus. Stronger bending of marginal rays is spherical aberration, which occurs even with monochromatic light. Diffraction is a separate effect set by the aperture size: a resolution limit that remains even with no aberrations.

geometric-008.question: Which statement about the spherical aberration of a single convex lens is correct?
choices: Rays passing farther from the optical axis come to a focus beyond the paraxial focus
Rays passing farther from the optical axis come to a focus closer to the lens than the paraxial focus
It does not occur with monochromatic light and appears only with white light
geometric-008.explanation: In a lens with spherical surfaces, marginal rays are refracted more strongly than the paraxial approximation predicts, so in a convex lens they focus in front of the paraxial focus (on the lens side). Saying marginal rays focus farther away reverses the sign; that is the behavior of a concave lens or an overcorrected system. Spherical aberration is a monochromatic aberration that arises from the geometry of refraction and is not limited to white light (a white-light-only problem is chromatic aberration). Remedies include aspheric lenses, sharing the bending between surfaces (a plano-convex lens with its curved side toward the collimated beam), splitting the power over several lenses, and stopping down the aperture.

geometric-009.question: Paraxial rays are represented by their height y and angle θ and traced with ABCD (ray transfer) matrices. For a system consisting of a thin lens of focal length f followed immediately by free space of length d, what is the A element of M = (free space)·(lens)? Use [[1, d], [0, 1]] for free space and [[1, 0], [−1/f, 1]] for the thin lens.
choices: 1 − d/f
1 + d/f
geometric-009.explanation: Matrices are multiplied from the right in the reverse of the order in which light passes through. M = [[1, d], [0, 1]]·[[1, 0], [−1/f, 1]] = [[1 − d/f, d], [−1/f, 1]], so A = 1 − d/f. A tells how the input ray height maps to the output height, and A = 0 when d = f: rays entering parallel to the axis meet on the axis (at the focus) regardless of their height. 1 + d/f is the result for a lens with the opposite sign of power, equivalent to a concave lens, and −1/f is the C element of this system. ABCD matrices can be used unchanged for Gaussian-beam propagation.

geometric-010.question: For the ABCD matrix of an optical system whose input and output are in media of the same refractive index, which relation always holds?
choices: A + D equals 1
The determinant AD − BC equals 1
The product of B and C equals −1
geometric-010.explanation: The determinant of an ABCD matrix equals the ratio of input to output refractive indices, n₁/n₂, so AD − BC = 1 when both are in the same medium. Free space [[1, d], [0, 1]] and a thin lens [[1, 0], [−1/f, 1]] both have determinant 1, and determinants multiply, so any combination of them also has determinant 1. This corresponds to conservation of the phase-space area occupied by a bundle of rays (étendue). A + D (the trace) varies from system to system and is used in the resonator stability condition |A + D|/2 ≤ 1. There is no general rule for the product of B and C.

geometric-011.question: You want to bend a beam by 90° using total internal reflection at the hypotenuse of a right-angle prism. In air, with an angle of incidence of 45° on the hypotenuse, which value is closest to the minimum refractive index the prism needs for total internal reflection?
choices: About 1.41
About 2.0
Anything greater than 1.0
geometric-011.explanation: Total internal reflection requires the angle of incidence to be at least the critical angle, that is, sin45° ≥ 1/n. So n ≥ 1/sin45° = √2 ≈ 1.41 is needed. Ordinary optical glass (about 1.52 for BK7) meets this condition and gives nearly 100% reflection without a reflective coating. About 2.0 is 1/sin30°, calculated as if the angle of incidence were 30°. “Anything greater than 1.0” (any index higher than air's) forgets the critical-angle condition: with an index of 1.3, for example, the critical angle is about 50°, so at 45° incidence most of the light passes out through the hypotenuse. Total-internal-reflection prisms reflect better than metal mirrors and degrade less, so they are used in binoculars, periscopes and for folding laser beam paths.

geometric-012.question: A 2 mm diameter laser beam is expanded with a Keplerian beam expander made of two convex lenses with focal lengths of 50 mm and 200 mm. Which correctly gives the output beam diameter and the lens spacing?
choices: 8 mm diameter, 150 mm lens spacing
0.5 mm diameter, 250 mm lens spacing
8 mm diameter, 250 mm lens spacing
geometric-012.explanation: A Keplerian expander places the two convex lenses so their foci coincide, so the spacing is f₁ + f₂ = 50 + 200 = 250 mm. The magnification is f₂/f₁ = 4, giving a diameter of 2 × 4 = 8 mm. A spacing of 150 mm is the difference f₂ − f₁, which applies to the Galilean type that uses a concave and a convex lens. A 0.5 mm diameter is the reduction you get with the lenses reversed (entering from the 200 mm side). Expanding the beam 4 times reduces its divergence to 1/4, giving a smaller spot far away or at a focus. The Keplerian type has an internal focus where a pinhole can serve as a spatial filter, but at high power air breakdown at that focus must be considered.

geometric-013.question: When using a passive optical system (a combination of lenses and mirrors) to couple light from an LED efficiently into an optical fiber with a small core, which statement correctly describes the constraint?
choices: Shortening the lens focal length shrinks the image without changing the spread of angles, so the light stays within the fiber's NA and coupling efficiency can be raised without limit
LED light has low coherence, so when a lens gathers it the light cancels itself at the focus and no bright spot forms
The product of source area and solid angle (étendue) cannot be reduced, so shrinking the image widens the angles, and light beyond the fiber's NA does not couple
geometric-013.explanation: A passive optical system cannot reduce the product of the area and solid angle occupied by a bundle of rays (étendue, also multiplied by the square of the refractive index). This is the same principle as the second law of thermodynamics and the conservation of radiance. If a source like an LED, with a large emitting area radiating over wide angles, is imaged down to a small spot, the ray angles widen by the same factor and spill outside the fiber's acceptance angle (NA). Changing the focal length preserves this trade-off between image reduction and angle expansion. Low coherence does not prevent focusing, but because of its large étendue, LED light hardly enters a single-mode fiber at all. This is why lasers, with their small étendue, are suited to fiber coupling.

geometric-014.question: Why are “object-side telecentric” lenses used for dimensional measurement by machine vision in factories?
choices: Because the chief rays are parallel to the axis, the magnification hardly changes even if the object shifts slightly along the axis
Because they have a very high numerical aperture, and aligning the chief rays gives resolution beyond the diffraction limit for reading fine dimensions
Because they have no chromatic aberration at all, so the focal length is the same at every wavelength and dimensions do not change with the illumination color
geometric-014.explanation: An object-side telecentric system places the aperture stop at the image-side focal point, which makes the chief ray from each object point (the ray through the center of the stop) parallel to the optical axis. If the object shifts in depth, the image blurs, but the center of the blur does not move, so the measured dimension (magnification) does not change. With an ordinary lens, perspective makes nearer objects appear larger, so dimensions change. Telecentricity is a property separate from NA and resolution and does not beat the diffraction limit. Chromatic aberration also has to be corrected separately in the design.

geometric-015.question: Thin lenses with focal lengths of 100 mm and 200 mm are placed in contact in air. Which correctly gives the optical power of the 100 mm lens (in diopters, D) and the combined focal length of the pair?
choices: 0.01 D, combined focal length 300 mm
10 D, combined focal length about 66.7 mm
10 D, combined focal length 150 mm
geometric-015.explanation: Optical power is the reciprocal of the focal length in meters: 1/0.1 m = 10 D. 0.01 D is the unit error of taking the reciprocal of the focal length in millimeters. For thin lenses in contact the powers add, so 10 D + 5 D = 15 D, and the combined focal length is 1/15 m ≈ 66.7 mm. 300 mm and 150 mm come from adding or averaging the focal lengths themselves, which contradicts the fact that stacking two lenses bends light more strongly (a shorter focal length). When the lenses are separated, 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/(f₁f₂), so the combined focal length depends on the spacing d.

geometric-016.question: A coin lies on the bottom of a pool 40 cm deep and is viewed from directly above. Which value is closest to the depth at which the coin appears (the apparent depth)? Take the refractive index of water as 1.33 and consider only rays close to the axis.
choices: About 53 cm
About 30 cm
40 cm (the same as the real depth)
geometric-016.explanation: Viewing from directly above allows the paraxial approximation. Rays from the bottom bend away from the normal at the water surface, so they seem to come from a shallower point, and the apparent depth is real depth/n = 40/1.33 ≈ 30 cm. About 53 cm comes from multiplying by the index instead of dividing, which reverses the direction in which light bends when it leaves water for air. The depth is unchanged only when the indices on both sides are equal. Viewed obliquely, the paraxial approximation fails and the bottom appears raised even more.

geometric-017.question: A small letter 30 mm from a convex lens (a magnifying glass) with a focal length of 50 mm is viewed through the lens. Which correctly describes the image that is seen?
choices: An inverted, magnified real image behind the lens that can also be projected on a screen
An upright, reduced virtual image on the same side as the object (in front of the lens)
An upright, magnified virtual image in front of the lens, on the object's side
geometric-017.explanation: When the object is inside the focal length (a < f), light leaving the lens diverges instead of converging, so no real image forms; a virtual image appears where the rays traced backward intersect. Putting a = 30 mm and f = 50 mm into 1/a + 1/b = 1/f gives b = −75 mm; the negative sign means a virtual image in front of the lens, and the magnification is 75/30 = 2.5, upright. An inverted real image forms only when the object is outside the focal length, and only real images can be projected on a screen. An upright reduced virtual image is what a concave lens produces; for an object inside the focal length of a convex lens the image is always magnified.

geometric-018.question: A thin biconvex lens is made of glass with a refractive index of 1.5, and both surfaces have a radius of curvature of 60 mm (R₁ = +60 mm, R₂ = −60 mm). Which value is closest to its focal length in air? Use the lensmaker's equation 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂).
choices: About 60 mm
About 30 mm
About 120 mm
geometric-018.explanation: 1/f = (1.5 − 1)(1/60 + 1/60) = 0.5 × 2/60 = 1/60, so f = 60 mm. In a biconvex lens both surfaces bend light toward the axis, so with the signs handled correctly their contributions add. About 30 mm comes from leaving out the factor (n − 1), which would contradict the fact that a lens with the same index as its surroundings does not bend light. About 120 mm counts only one surface. Higher-index glass and more strongly curved surfaces shorten the focal length, and when the surrounding index rises, as in water, the index difference shrinks and the focal length becomes longer.

geometric-019.question: A concave front-surface mirror (a metal coating on the surface of the glass) with a radius of curvature of 200 mm focuses a collimated beam of white light. Compared with a single lens of the same focal length, which correctly describes the concave mirror?
choices: Its focal length is about 200 mm, and dispersion in the glass in front of the mirror gives it more chromatic aberration than a single lens
Its focal length is about 100 mm, but because the reflectance of the metal film varies with wavelength, the focus shifts with color
Its focal length is about 100 mm, and since the direction of reflection does not depend on wavelength, it has no chromatic aberration
geometric-019.explanation: For a spherical mirror the paraxial focal length is f = R/2, so a radius of 200 mm gives about 100 mm. In reflection the direction of light is set only by the law that the angles of incidence and reflection are equal, with no refractive index involved, so all wavelengths meet at the same point and there is no chromatic aberration. This is one reason reflecting mirrors are common in astronomical telescopes and infrared or ultraviolet spectrometers. Taking the focal length equal to the radius is wrong, and in a front-surface mirror the light does not pass through glass. Even if the reflectance of the metal film varies with wavelength, the ray directions do not, so the focus does not shift. A spherical mirror still has spherical aberration, and a parabolic mirror is used to bring a collimated beam to a single point.

geometric-020.question: On a sunny summer day, the road ahead on hot asphalt sometimes looks like a puddle reflecting the sky (an inferior mirage). Which correctly explains this?
choices: The hot air near the road has a higher refractive index, and grazing light is totally reflected in that layer, so the road mirrors the sky
The hot air near the road has a lower refractive index, and light bends upward toward the higher index, so light from the sky seems to come from the road
Water vapor rising from the hot road forms a thin film of water on its surface, and reflection from that film shows the sky
geometric-020.explanation: The refractive index of air exceeds 1 by an amount proportional to its density, so it decreases as the temperature rises. The layer next to the road has the lowest index, and in a medium whose index varies continuously a ray bends toward the higher index, that is, upward, so skylight heading toward the road at a grazing angle turns back toward the eye. The eye places the image along the direction from which the light arrives, so the sky appears to lie on the road. Saying the hot air has a higher index gets the direction backward. The effect also occurs on a dry road, so it is not reflection from a water film. Bending light with an index gradient is the same idea used in GRIN lenses.

geometric-021.question: Which statement correctly describes Fermat's principle, which determines the path a light ray takes?
choices: The path between two points is the one for which the optical path length (the integral of index × distance) is stationary, usually a minimum
The path of light between two points is the straight line of shortest geometric distance, independent of the refractive index of the media along the way
The path of light between two points is the one that takes the longest time, so the light travels as far as possible through the high-index medium
geometric-021.explanation: According to Fermat's principle, light follows the path for which the optical path length L = ∫n ds is stationary (unchanged to first order when the path is varied slightly). Dividing the optical path length by the vacuum speed of light gives the travel time, so in most cases this is the path of least time. Applying this condition at a boundary between two media of different index gives Snell's law, n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, and at a mirror it gives the law of reflection. Light follows the straight line of shortest geometric distance only inside a uniform medium; at a boundary it bends so as to travel a longer distance on the low-index side. Saying that light chooses the path of longest time gets it backward, and light does not prefer to travel long distances through a high-index medium.

geometric-022.question: Monochromatic light passes through a glass prism with an apex angle of 60° and a refractive index of 1.5. Which value is closest to the angle of minimum deviation δmin? (Use the minimum-deviation condition n = sin((A + δmin)/2) / sin(A/2), where A is the apex angle.)
choices: About 30°
About 37°
About 49°
geometric-022.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes through the prism parallel to its base, symmetrically. Rearranging the condition gives sin((A + δmin)/2) = n sin(A/2) = 1.5 × sin30° = 0.75, so (A + δmin)/2 ≈ 48.6° and δmin ≈ 2 × 48.6° − 60° ≈ 37.2°. About 30° comes from applying the thin-prism approximation δ ≈ (n − 1)A to a 60° apex angle; for a large apex angle this approximation fails and underestimates the deviation. About 49° mistakes the angle (A + δmin)/2 itself for the deviation. Because the minimum deviation can be measured precisely, it is used to determine the refractive index of glass (the minimum-deviation method).

geometric-023.question: A thin lens forms a real image of an object with a lateral magnification of −2. If the object is moved by just 1 mm along the optical axis, which value is closest to the distance the image moves along the axis? (Assume paraxial optics and a small displacement.)
choices: About 1 mm
About 2 mm
About 4 mm
geometric-023.explanation: Differentiating the imaging equation 1/a + 1/b = 1/f gives −da/a² − db/b² = 0, so db = −(b/a)² da. The magnification along the axis (the longitudinal magnification) is the square m² of the lateral magnification m = −b/a, so for m = −2 it is 4, and moving the object by 1 mm moves the image by about 4 mm. As the object approaches the lens the image moves away from it, that is, both move in the same direction relative to the direction of the light. About 2 mm wrongly applies the size of the lateral magnification to depth as well, and about 1 mm assumes that the image moves as far as the object. In a magnified image, depth is stretched even more than the transverse size, so in a high-magnification system such as a microscope a small shift on the object side becomes a large focus shift on the image side.

geometric-024.question: Which statement correctly describes a corner cube (corner reflector), made of three mutually perpendicular mirrors (or totally reflecting faces)?
choices: Even if the incident direction changes somewhat, three reflections send the light back antiparallel to the incident direction
As with a plane mirror, tilting the element by an angle α shifts the direction of the returned light by 2α, so precise angular alignment is needed
The three mirrors act like a concave mirror, so a collimated beam is focused to a point in front of the corner where the faces meet
geometric-024.explanation: Successive reflections from three mutually perpendicular surfaces reverse the sign of each component of the propagation vector (kx, ky, kz) in turn, ending with (−kx, −ky, −kz). As a result, even if the element is tilted somewhat, the light returns antiparallel to the incident direction (with a small lateral offset). This is why corner cubes are used as surveying reflectors, in the retroreflectors placed on the Moon, and in delay lines for interferometers and pump-probe measurements. A shift of twice the tilt angle is the behavior of a single plane mirror; a corner cube needs almost no angular alignment. A combination of flat surfaces has no optical power, so it does not focus a collimated beam either.

geometric-025.question: Convex mirrors are used for car side mirrors and for traffic mirrors at blind corners. Which correctly describes the image formed by a convex mirror? (The object is a real object in front of the mirror.)
choices: An object beyond the focal point gives an inverted real image and a closer object gives an upright virtual image, so the orientation depends on the distance
Regardless of the object position, an upright, reduced virtual image forms behind the mirror, so a wide area can be seen at once
Regardless of the object position, an upright, magnified virtual image forms behind the mirror, so distant cars look larger
geometric-025.explanation: The focal point of a convex mirror lies behind the mirror, and its focal length f = −R/2 is negative. Putting a positive object distance a into the imaging equation 1/a + 1/b = 1/f always gives a negative b with |b| < |f|, so an upright, reduced virtual image forms behind the mirror, inside the focal point. Because the image is small, a wide area can be seen at once, but objects seem farther away than they really are. Switching between an inverted real image and an upright virtual image depending on the object position is the behavior of a concave mirror. An upright, magnified virtual image is also produced by a concave mirror (such as a makeup mirror) with the object inside its focal point; a convex mirror always gives a reduced image.
